Table 8: Depth ordering accuracy for various pictorial depth cues. Synthetic (all cue strengths): mean accuracy across all cue strengths for each individual depth cue (HP: Height-in-Plane, OC: Occlusion, RS: Relative Size, TG: Texture Gradient, SA: Saturation, LS: Light-and-Shadow, FO: Focusness, FS: Familiar Size); Synthetic: accuracy averaged over all images with the same number of cues; Real-world : accuracy averaged over all images with the same number of cues.

Fig. 5: Comparison of depth ordering accuracies as cue strengths double, for each cue and each VLM. Grey dashed lines are chance level (0.5). The double cue strength is not applicable to the Familiar Size (FS) cue.

Fig. 1: O3-D probes VLM depth and language understanding. We start by constructing synthetic and real 3D scenes with diverse backgrounds and objects. Each scene contains 5 objects of the same class, one of which (the target) is of different size and placed at a different depth plane. We then generate a number of 2D views with one or two depth cues by controlling the camera, light position, etc. For each image, we create prompt variations: multiple-choice (shown in green) and yes-no (yellow). Within each prompt, we vary the target referring clarity (more specific references are shown in darker shades of blue in the Target ref. variations box) and distractor descriptions (Distractor ref. variations).

Fig. 3: Image post-processing. (a) Resize a real image to 1024 × 683. (b) Optionally add markers for easier referring (Tab. 3 bottom row), to gauge the effects of referring expression comprehension (REC) on depth ordering responses.
Fig. 6: A heatmap showing Spearman’s rank correlation among single cues. The ranks of the depth ordering accuracies of VLMs are used to compute the correlation.
Fig. 2: Cropping images. (a) Odd-one-out image before cropping. (b) Cropped images specifically for the depth ordering task.

Table 11: Depth ordering accuracy with respect to referring clarity. The VLM mean improvements due to increased clarity are marginal. Kosmos2’s referring by bounding box does not boost accuracy either.

Table 10: Influence of yes-no questions on positive answers. Numbers in the two middle columns are target-far accuracy, AccF , for multi-choice and yes-no questions, respectively. The difference is defined as yes-no minus multi-choice. A positive Diff means the model prefers answering “yes” to yes-no questions, and vice versa. Only DeepSeek-VL prefers answering “no”.

Table 9: Response inconsistency influenced by question variations. First 5 columns represent modified SDGMs for specific types of question variations (described earlier in Tab. 4). The last column contains SDGMs across all 42 question variations. Lower SDGM is better.
Fig. 4: Mean depth ordering accuracy by models and number of cues (aggregated across the 14 environments). Error bars denote 95% CIs. Most VLMs perform at chance level.
